# Software Subscription Transition Roadmap

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This roadmap manages a **high-stakes business model transition** that creates a predictable revenue cliff, misaligned incentives, and customer entitlement risk. The strategy balances three conflicting imperatives:

1. **Revenue stability** – Minimize the subscription trough and shorten its duration
2. **Customer retention** – Hold the installed base (competitor lost 20% + churn compounds)
3. **Organizational alignment** – Realign sales incentives, forecast credibility, and investor expectations before the transition begins

**Core thesis:** The competitor's 20% loss wasn't inevitable—it resulted from poor offer design, rushed migration, and sales force sabotage. With intentional architecture (3-tier migration path, earnings protection, transparent runway), you can achieve 80%+ retention and emerge with a healthier, more valuable business model.

---

## 1. SITUATION ANALYSIS & TRANSITION RISKS

### 1.1 Financial & Strategic Context

```
REVENUE MODEL DIAGNOSIS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT STATE (PERPETUAL LICENSE + UPGRADES):
├─ Revenue pattern: Lumpy, deal-driven
│  ├─ Large upfront license fee ($50K–$500K+, depending on enterprise size)
│  ├─ Upgrade revenue: 20–30% of customer base upgrades annually (3–5 years between upgrades)
│  ├─ Average deal size: Growing as customer base matures
│  ├─ Sales cycle: 3–9 months (long, but paid upfront)
│  └─ Unpredictable: Q3 may be 3x Q2 (customer budgets, forecasting nightmare)
│
├─ Revenue quality (investor perspective):
│  ├─ Perceived as: "Legacy model, low-growth, concentrated risk"
│  ├─ Valuation multiple: Likely 3–5x revenue (software/SaaS average: 6–10x)
│  ├─ Investor concern: Lumpy revenue = lower margins, less predictable, higher risk
│  ├─ Upgrade cycles: Getting longer as product matures (customers delay upgrades)
│  └─ Competitive pressure: New competitors w/ SaaS models valued at 8–12x revenue
│
├─ Customer relationship:
│  ├─ Entitlement: "I bought the license, I own it forever"
│  ├─ Upgrade reluctance: "Why pay for upgrades when current license works?"
│  ├─ Switching cost: Low (perpetual licenses are portable, not locked in)
│  ├─ Loyalty: Moderate; customer switching to SaaS competitors common
│  └─ Support expectations: "Free or minimal cost" (not monthly service mindset)

SUBSCRIPTION MODEL (TARGET):
├─ Revenue pattern: Predictable, recurring, growing
│  ├─ Monthly/annual subscription: $500–$5K+/month (depending on tier)
│  ├─ Churn assumption: 5–10% annual (industry standard, with good product/support)
│  ├─ Expansion revenue: Upsells, seat growth, feature add-ons = 15–25% annual
│  ├─ New customer acquisition: Only via subscription (no more perpetual deals)
│  ├─ Sales cycle: 1–3 months (shorter, monthly commitment = lower barrier)
│  └─ Predictability: Month-to-month visibility; investor-friendly
│
├─ Revenue quality (investor perspective):
│  ├─ Perceived as: "Modern, growth-oriented, predictable, sticky"
│  ├─ Valuation multiple: 8–12x revenue (SaaS standard; 2–3x higher than perpetual)
│  ├─ ARR (annual recurring revenue): Higher quality metric than lumpy upfront fees
│  ├─ LTV (lifetime value): Higher multiples for recurring revenue models
│  ├─ Growth potential: Subscription ARR grows 20–30%+ annually (vs. upgrade cycles)
│  └─ Exit appeal: Strategic buyers and PE firms prefer SaaS models
│
├─ Customer relationship:
│  ├─ Expectation shift: From "I own it" to "I rent it and expect regular updates"
│  ├─ Upgrade frequency: Monthly/quarterly (much higher product velocity)
│  ├─ Support expectations: 24/7, responsive (service mentality embedded)
│  ├─ Lock-in: Monthly commitment = stickier (but also higher churn risk if unhappy)
│  └─ Expansion: Easier to add users/features (growth lever vs. one-time deal)

TRANSITION TROUGH (THE CORE PROBLEM):
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

REVENUE SHAPE DURING TRANSITION:
Year 0 (Current)          │ Year 1                │ Year 2                │ Year 3+
Perpetual + upgrades      │ Mixed revenue         │ Mostly subscription   │ Pure subscription
$50M baseline (100%)      │ Trough begins         │ Trough ends          │ $55M+ (growth)
                          │
                          ├─ Perpetual: $40M     ├─ Perpetual: $15M     ├─ Perpetual: $2M
                          ├─ New subs: $5M       ├─ New subs: $35M      ├─ New subs: $48M
                          ├─ Migration credits   ├─ Migration credits   ├─ (full migration)
                          ├─ Total: $45M (90%)   ├─ Total: $48M (96%)   ├─ Total: $50M+ (growth)
                          └─ TROUGH: -10%        └─ RECOVERY: +4%       └─ Growth kicks in

TROUGH CHARACTERISTICS:
├─ Depth: 10–20% revenue decline in Y1–Y2 (vs. baseline)
├─ Duration: 18–24 months (until subscription ARR exceeds perpetual revenue decline)
├─ Drivers:
│  ├─ Existing customers on perpetual deals (not generating upfront fees)
│  ├─ Migration discounts/credits (convert to lower initial ARPU on subs)
│  ├─ New customer acquisition slower (sales cycle shifts, new messaging)
│  ├─ Upgrade revenue vanishes (customers migrate to subs, don't buy upgrades)
│  └─ Compounding: Slower growth in trough = missed bookings = delayed recovery
│
├─ Investor/board reaction:
│  ├─ "Wait, we're making LESS money for the next 2 years?"
│  ├─ "Why would we do this if revenue goes down?"
│  ├─ "Competitor failed. Why won't we?"
│  ├─ "Is this a strategy or a business error?"
│  └─ Board may lose confidence → push for ROI, cut spend, halt transition → DISASTER
│
└─ Sales force reaction:
   ├─ "My $500K perpetual deal just became $60K annual subscription"
   ├─ "My commission is cut by 60% on the same customer"
   ├─ "Why would I sell subscriptions when perpetual pays more?"
   ├─ Result: Sales force sabotage—ignore subs, push perpetual deals harder → mixed revenue longer
   └─ Alternative outcome: Top sales reps leave for competitors → churn accelerates

COMPETITOR'S FAILURE (WARNING CASE):
├─ What happened:
│  ├─ Abrupt transition: "All new deals are SaaS only; existing perpetual customers on their own"
│  ├─ Poor migration offer: "You can migrate to subscription, but at full price (no discount)"
│  ├─ Sales force misalignment: No comp redesign; reps pushed perpetual deals longer
│  ├─ Customer surprise: No proactive education; "Why am I losing support if I don't subscribe?"
│  ├─ Result: 20% of installed base defected to competitors w/ perpetual options
│  └─ Timeline: 18 months to recovery; company credibility damaged
│
└─ Root causes of failure:
   ├─ Lack of intentional migration path → customers felt abandoned
   ├─ Misaligned sales incentives → reps opposed transition
   ├─ No investor/board buy-in on trough → pressure to abandon transition midway
   ├─ Weak customer communication → confusion, not strategy
   └─ Timing: Rushed launch, no runway for internal alignment

YOUR ADVANTAGE:
├─ You see the trap; competitor fell in it → opportunity to learn and avoid
├─ Transition is planned, not reactive → time to build offer, incentives, communication
├─ If executed well, you can hold 80–90% of base and grow from higher valuation
└─ If executed poorly, you lose 20% + suffer reputational damage + muddle for 3+ years

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### 1.2 Customer Segments & Entitlement Risk

```
INSTALLED BASE ANALYSIS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Assume current perpetual customer base: ~500 customers (mix of sizes)
Revenue distribution: Top 20% of customers = 80% of revenue (typical software)

CUSTOMER SEGMENTATION (by entitlement risk + migration ease):

SEGMENT A: "STRATEGIC ENTERPRISE" (20% of customer count, 50% of revenue)
├─ Profile:
│  ├─ Customer size: 500–50,000+ employees; Fortune 500 / large public companies
│  ├─ License spend: $100K–$500K+ upfront; $20K–$100K+ annual upgrades
│  ├─ Tenure: 5–15+ years with company; deeply integrated into workflow
│  ├─ Entitlement: VERY HIGH - "We own this license forever; we're core to your business"
│  ├─ Switching cost: HIGH - embedded in processes, trained users, integrations
│  ├─ Procurement: Centralized, contract-savvy; will negotiate hard
│  ├─ Support expectations: Premium; expect technical account managers, SLAs
│  └─ Decision maker: CFO/CTO (cost-sensitive, risk-averse)
│
├─ Transition risk:
│  ├─ HIGHEST churn risk if mishandled (but also HIGHEST value to retain)
│  ├─ Will demand: Long transition runway, special pricing, service guarantees
│  ├─ May have: Multi-year budget cycles; procurement freeze until next cycle (6+ months)
│  ├─ Likely reaction: "Show us the business case; we're not moving until we're convinced"
│  └─ Churn cost: Losing even 5% of this segment = $2.5M+ revenue loss
│
├─ Migration approach:
│  ├─ Strategy: WHITE-GLOVE TRANSITION
│  ├─ Timeline: 18–24 month migration window per customer (not forced)
│  ├─ Offer: Custom pricing, extended trial, dedicated technical transition support
│  ├─ Economic model: True-up pricing (first year at/below current total cost of ownership)
│  ├─ Success metric: 90%+ retention in this segment
│  └─ Effort: High-touch; each customer is strategic deal

SEGMENT B: "ESTABLISHED MID-MARKET" (30% of count, 35% of revenue)
├─ Profile:
│  ├─ Customer size: 100–5,000 employees; mid-sized companies
│  ├─ License spend: $20K–$100K upfront; $5K–$20K annual upgrades
│  ├─ Tenure: 3–8 years with company; reasonably integrated
│  ├─ Entitlement: MODERATE-HIGH - "We've been loyal; treat us fairly"
│  ├─ Switching cost: MODERATE - Would migrate if pain outweighs benefit
│  ├─ Procurement: Mix of centralized/departmental; some negotiation
│  ├─ Support expectations: Standard; responsive but not premium
│  └─ Decision maker: Manager/Director (balance of cost and ease)
│
├─ Transition risk:
│  ├─ MEDIUM-HIGH risk; some will migrate, some will hold perpetual licenses
│  ├─ Price-sensitive; will shop alternatives if migration costs too much
│  ├─ May require: Simple economics (e.g., "subscription at ~70% of perpetual total cost")
│  ├─ Window: 12–18 month migration is acceptable
│  └─ Churn risk: ~10–15% may try alternatives if offer feels unfair
│
├─ Migration approach:
│  ├─ Strategy: STRUCTURED MIGRATION OFFER (standard tier, clear incentives)
│  ├─ Timeline: 12–18 months per customer
│  ├─ Offer: Tiered subscription pricing, 1-year lock-in optional, migration discount (10–20%)
│  ├─ Economic model: Clear cost comparison (perpetual + upgrades vs. subscription)
│  ├─ Success metric: 80–85% retention
│  └─ Effort: Scalable; leverage templates, self-service tools, account management

SEGMENT C: "GROWTH / NEWER CUSTOMERS" (30% of count, 12% of revenue)
├─ Profile:
│  ├─ Customer size: 10–500 employees; smaller companies
│  ├─ License spend: $5K–$50K upfront; $2K–$10K annual upgrades
│  ├─ Tenure: 1–4 years; integrated but less sticky
│  ├─ Entitlement: LOW-MODERATE - "We got a good deal, but we're flexible"
│  ├─ Switching cost: LOW - Easily replace with competitor SaaS offering
│  ├─ Procurement: Fast-moving, opportunistic; cost-sensitive
│  ├─ Support expectations: Self-service + ticketing; not premium
│  └─ Decision maker: Manager/User (ease of use, cost, flexibility)
│
├─ Transition risk:
│  ├─ MEDIUM churn risk; less attached to legacy model
│  ├─ Will migrate if subscription pricing attractive (vs. competitor SaaS)
│  ├─ May require: Aggressive pricing, freemium/trial option, ease of migration
│  ├─ Window: 6–12 month migration acceptable (faster decision-making)
│  └─ Opportunity: This segment is most SaaS-ready; highest conversion rate possible
│
├─ Migration approach:
│  ├─ Strategy: SELF-SERVICE + INCENTIVE (low-touch, high-velocity)
│  ├─ Timeline: 6–12 months
│  ├─ Offer: Standard subscription tiers, trial period (30–60 days free), migration incentive (15–25% discount or 1 free month)
│  ├─ Economic model: Transparent, online pricing; no custom deals
│  ├─ Success metric: 75–80% conversion; faster cycle
│  └─ Effort: Mostly automated; email campaigns, self-service portal, chatbot support

SEGMENT D: "LEGACY / AT-RISK" (20% of count, 3% of revenue)
├─ Profile:
│  ├─ Customer size: Varied; often inactive or declining user base
│  ├─ License spend: $1K–$20K (old deal); rarely upgrade ($0–$2K annually)
│  ├─ Tenure: 5–15+ years; often integrated into legacy systems
│  ├─ Entitlement: HIGH - "We own this forever; shouldn't have to pay monthly"
│  ├─ Switching cost: HIGH (entrenched, legacy systems) OR LOW (barely using product)
│  ├─ Procurement: Often unresponsive; old contacts; budget already allocated to upgrade
│  ├─ Support expectations: Minimal; only contact support when critical
│  └─ Decision maker: Original buyer (may have left company); hard to reach
│
├─ Transition risk:
│  ├─ LIKELY CHURN (30–50%) - Low revenue, low attachment, high friction
│  ├─ Unlikely to migrate unless very easy (and maybe not even then)
│  ├─ Win-back cost > lifetime value (probably not worth aggressive retention)
│  ├─ Opportunity: Identify which are truly inactive (should probably end relationship)
│  └─ Time cost: Don't spend much energy here; prioritize A/B/C segments
│
├─ Migration approach:
│  ├─ Strategy: SUNSET + SELECTIVE WIN-BACK
│  ├─ Timeline: 12 months to deprecation; no aggressive retention push
│  ├─ Offer: Heavily discounted subscription (e.g., "first year free, then $X/month") to win back engaged customers
│  ├─ Outreach: Single email campaign + support response if they inquire
│  ├─ Success metric: 25–30% retention acceptable (clear out deadweight)
│  └─ Effort: Minimal; automate communication; manually pursue only if customer responds

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

INSTALLED BASE MIGRATION TARGETS (by segment):
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Segment       │ Count │ % Rev │ Churn Risk │ Retention   │ Avg Deal  │ Retention
              │       │       │            │ Target      │ Value     │ $ Value
──────────────┼───────┼───────┼────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────
A (Enterprise)│ 100   │ 50%   │ Very High  │ 90%         │ $250K     │ $22.5M
B (Mid-Market)│ 150   │ 35%   │ Medium     │ 82%         │ $50K      │ $6.15M
C (Growth)    │ 150   │ 12%   │ Medium     │ 78%         │ $8K       │ $936K
D (Legacy)    │ 100   │ 3%    │ Very High  │ 30%         │ $1.5K     │ $45K
──────────────┼───────┼───────┼────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────
TOTAL         │ 500   │ 100%  │ —          │ ~80%*       │ $81.6K    │ $29.6M
                                                 *Average retention

Current perpetual revenue: $40.8M (500 customers × $81.6K avg)
Predicted post-migration perpetual retention: $29.6M (80% of customer base, similar upfront value)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

---

## 2. OFFER STRUCTURE & CUSTOMER MIGRATION PATH

### 2.1 Three-Tier Migration Architecture

```
MIGRATION OFFER FRAMEWORK (3 PATHS DESIGNED FOR DIFFERENT CUSTOMER PROFILES)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PRINCIPLE: Give customers choice + clear economics to avoid feeling "forced"

PATH 1: "PERPETUAL LEGACY TRACK" (For customers unwilling to transition)
├─ Duration: Available through end of Year 2 (24-month window)
├─ What it is:
│  ├─ Customers can keep perpetual licenses as-is
│  ├─ BUT: No new features, security updates only, minimal support
│  ├─ Can stay perpetual indefinitely (no forced sunset)
│  ├─ Cost: Current license + optional annual support ($X/year for basic support)
│  └─ Messaging: "Keep your license. Support continues. But innovation moves to subscription."
│
├─ Target customers:
│  ├─ Segment D (legacy, low engagement) - accept churn, keep on minimal cost
│  ├─ Segment A (enterprise, highly price-sensitive) - let them stay if they insist, but transition path better
│  ├─ Decision driver: "I don't want to change anything; I'll stay perpetual even if stagnant"
│  └─ Expected adoption: 10–15% of base (mostly legacy customers)
│
├─ Economics:
│  ├─ Revenue: $4–6M annually (from customers choosing to stay perpetual + minimal support)
│  ├─ Margin: HIGH (no product investment, minimal support, mainly license maintenance)
│  ├─ Risk: Perpetual customer base shrinks slowly; predictable; not growth lever
│  └─ Strategic purpose:
│     ├─ Removes "forced conversion" narrative (customer choice)
│     ├─ Buys time for hesitant customers to get comfortable with SaaS
│     ├─ Keeps some revenue vs. losing customers entirely
│     └─ Allows pivot-to-subscription without perceived bait-and-switch
│
└─ Implementation:
   ├─ Offer letter: "Your license is perpetual. We will continue to provide critical security updates."
   ├─ Support tier: Basic (bug fixes, critical issues only; no enhancements)
   ├─ Communication: "We're investing in the future through subscription. Perpetual licenses get baseline support."
   ├─ Compliance: No special treatment; treat like any legacy product line (e.g., Windows XP support model)
   └─ Sunset trigger: If <5% of revenue in perpetual track by Year 3, begin formal EOL roadmap

PATH 2: "GUIDED MIGRATION OFFER" (For customers open to subscription with incentives)
├─ Duration: Primary migration window = 12–18 months; extended window through Year 2
├─ What it is:
│  ├─ Customers migrate from perpetual license to annual/monthly subscription
│  ├─ First year (migration year): Special pricing to make case
│  ├─ Year 2+: Standard subscription pricing (aligned with new customers)
│  ├─ All features available; ongoing updates, support, new capabilities
│  ├─ Optional multi-year commitment (1–3 years) for cost predictability
│  └─ Messaging: "Upgrade to modern SaaS. Pay less Year 1. Better support, faster innovation."
│
├─ Pricing structure:
│  ├─ Subscription tiers (detailed later): Startup ($500/mo), Business ($2K/mo), Enterprise ($5K+/mo)
│  ├─ Migration discount: Customers get credit/reduction equal to ~X% of perpetual deal value (see Tier A/B below)
│  └─ Examples:
│     ├─ Enterprise: Paid $300K for perpetual license + $30K/year upgrades for last 3 years = $90K/year TCO
│     │                 Migrates to Enterprise tier subscription: Year 1 = $80K/year (10% below TCO)
│     │                 Year 2+ = $90K/year (aligned with TCO)
│     ├─ Mid-Market: Paid $40K license + $6K/year upgrades = $8K/year TCO
│     │                 Migrates to Business tier: Year 1 = $7K/year (12% below)
│     │                 Year 2+ = $8–9K/year (slightly above, for faster innovation)
│     └─ Growth: Paid $8K license + $1.5K/year upgrades = $2.5K/year TCO
│                   Migrates to Startup tier: Year 1 = $2K/year (20% below; attract early movers)
│                   Year 2+ = $2.5–3K/year (slight increase, still good value)
│
├─ Target customers:
│  ├─ Segment A (enterprise, 90% target): Customers willing to move if ROI clear
│  ├─ Segment B (mid-market, 82% target): Price-conscious, want clear business case
│  ├─ Segment C (growth, 78% target): Already SaaS-minded, easiest conversion
│  └─ Decision driver: "The subscription offer is good value compared to what I'm paying now"
│
├─ Incentives (by segment):
│  │
│  ├─ TIER A (STRATEGIC ENTERPRISE): 
│  │  ├─ Migration credit: Up to 15–20% discount on Year 1 subscription
│  │  ├─ Example: Customer currently at $100K/year TCO → migrates to $85K/year for Year 1, then $100K+
│  │  ├─ Lock-in: Optional 2–3 year contract at locked price (protects forecast)
│  │  ├─ Service: Dedicated technical account manager + quarterly business reviews
│  │  ├─ Migration support: Dedicated transition technician (on your dime)
│  │  ├─ SLA guarantee: 99.5% uptime, 4-hour support response (vs. standard 24-hour)
│  │  ├─ Cost to you: High (personalized support, custom pricing, deep discounts)
│  │  ├─ Revenue impact: Lower Year 1, but locked in Year 2–3 = predictable, high-value ARR
│  │  ├─ Churn risk: Very low if handled well; these customers are valuable
│  │  └─ Effort: High-touch sales, legal negotiation, onboarding (1 person per deal)
│  │
│  ├─ TIER B (ESTABLISHED MID-MARKET):
│  │  ├─ Migration credit: 10–15% discount on Year 1 subscription
│  │  ├─ Example: $40K license + $6K/year upgrades = $8K TCO → $7K Year 1, $8.5K+ Year 2
│  │  ├─ Lock-in: Optional 1–2 year contract at locked price
│  │  ├─ Service: Standard technical account manager + semi-annual check-ins
│  │  ├─ Migration support: Shared transition resources (not 1:1, but guided)
│  │  ├─ SLA guarantee: 99% uptime, 8-hour support response (standard SaaS)
│  │  ├─ Cost to you: Medium (some customization, standard pricing discount)
│  │  ├─ Revenue impact: Moderate Year 1 discount, strong Year 2+ recurring ARR
│  │  ├─ Churn risk: Medium; price-sensitive, may shop alternatives
│  │  └─ Effort: Medium-touch (sales team + onboarding, but scalable)
│  │
│  └─ TIER C (GROWTH / NEWER CUSTOMERS):
│     ├─ Migration credit: 15–25% discount on Year 1 subscription (aggressive)
│     ├─ Example: $8K license + $1.5K/year = $2.5K TCO → $2K Year 1, $2.5K+ Year 2
│     ├─ Lock-in: Optional 1-year contract; month-to-month if preferred
│     ├─ Service: Standard support + access to customer community
│     ├─ Migration support: Self-service portal + email support
│     ├─ SLA guarantee: 99% uptime, standard response times
│     ├─ Cost to you: Low (self-service, standard pricing, high volume)
│     ├─ Revenue impact: Low Year 1 (discounts attract volume), growing Year 2+
│     ├─ Churn risk: Medium-high (low switching cost, price-sensitive, but SaaS-native)
│     └─ Effort: Mostly automated (email campaigns, self-service, minimal touch)
│
├─ Timeline & mechanics:
│  ├─ Announcement: Company announces subscription offering, migration window
│  ├─ Month 1–3: Sales team begins outreach to Tier A customers (highest priority)
│  │             Self-service portal opened for Tier B/C customers
│  ├─ Month 3–12: Tier A migrations complete (majority) or in contract negotiation
│  │              Tier B migrations rolling (monthly); Tier C mostly self-service
│  ├─ Month 12–18: Tail of Tier A, bulk of Tier B complete
│  │               Tier C steady self-service
│  ├─ Month 18–24: Extended window; migration offers close (unless special case)
│  │               Perpetual legacy track activates for holdouts
│  └─ Year 3+: Subscription is dominant; perpetual is small tail
│
└─ Success criteria:
   ├─ Tier A: 90% retention, average $85K ARR (vs. current $100K TCO, acceptable Year 1)
   ├─ Tier B: 82% retention, average $8.5K ARR (slightly higher than TCO, justified by innovation)
   ├─ Tier C: 78% retention, average $2.5K ARR (Year 1 cheaper, Year 2 equivalent)
   └─ Overall installed base: 80% retention, blended ARR = $29.6M

PATH 3: "EXPANSION UPGRADE" (For customers ready to commit beyond replacement value)
├─ Duration: Available ongoing; primary focus Year 1–3
├─ What it is:
│  ├─ Premium subscription tier with enhanced capabilities
│  ├─ Targets customers who want more than legacy license provided
│  ├─ Positioned as: "Subscription + Add-ons" (not just replacement)
│  ├─ Can include: Advanced features, unlimited users, integrations, API access, etc.
│  └─ Messaging: "Unlock capabilities that perpetual license never had."
│
├─ Target customers:
│  ├─ Power users in Segment A (enterprise) - use advanced features
│  ├─ Growing organizations in Segment B/C - need more functionality as business scales
│  ├─ Any customer wanting to deepen product usage (expansion revenue)
│  └─ Decision driver: "Subscription enables us to use the product more strategically"
│
├─ Pricing & positioning:
│  ├─ Example tiers:
│  │  ├─ Starter: $500/mo (core features, 1–5 users)
│  │  ├─ Professional: $2K/mo (+ advanced features, 6–50 users)
│  │  ├─ Enterprise: $5K+/mo (+ premium support, unlimited users, custom integrations)
│  │  └─ Premium add-ons: +$500–$2K/mo (API access, advanced reporting, dedicated support)
│  │
│  ├─ Revenue lever: Average migrating customer starts at "Replacement" tier (matching current TCO)
│  │                 But 10–15% upgrade to "Professional" or "Enterprise" within Year 1–2
│  │                 This creates expansion revenue (15–25% annual growth above baseline)
│  └─ Example:
│     ├─ Enterprise customer at $100K/year perpetual
│     ├─ Migrates to $85K subscription Year 1 (discounted)
│     ├─ Year 2: Locks in $100K (back to TCO)
│     ├─ Year 3: Upgrades to Premium tier due to new features = $130K+
│     └─ Result: LTV increases despite migration discount
│
└─ Strategic purpose:
   ├─ Expansion revenue compensates for migration discounts in Year 1
